olig-012.title: Antarctica freezes and an ice age begins
olig-012.text: The ice age you live in today began about 33.9 million years ago, when ice started to build up on Antarctica. That moment opened the Late Cenozoic Ice Age, and it has never ended. The Eocene–Oligocene boundary marks the switch: Earth left its last greenhouse climate and entered the present icehouse, a world with permanent ice at the poles. The main driver was falling carbon dioxide. Once it dropped past a tipping point of about 600 ppm, the Antarctic ice could grow and persist. The north was not spared. Ice-rafted debris, rock dropped on the seafloor by melting icebergs, shows that glaciers had also appeared on Greenland by the start of the Oligocene. For the first time in the Phanerozoic, both poles fell well below freezing at once. Much of what follows in this chapter, from falling seas to spreading grasslands, traces back to this cold turn.

olig-008.title: Ground sloths appear and reach the Caribbean
olig-008.text: A single femur from Puerto Rico shows that ground sloths had reached the Caribbean by 31 million years ago. The earliest unambiguous ground-sloth fossils come from the early Oligocene, so the group spread fast. By about 30 million years ago the megatheriids had appeared in South America, the family that would later produce the giant ground sloths.

olig-001.title: Africa pushes north and the Alps rise
olig-001.text: Africa kept shoving north into Eurasia, and the crust between them buckled upward. The Alps rose rapidly, and as they did they cut off the remnants of the old Tethys Sea. Most Alpine mountain building happened in the Oligocene and Miocene. The rising range shed its debris northward. From about 30 to 10 million years ago, shallow-marine and continental sediment filled the Molasse basin, a long trough along the northern foot of the Alps. That basin is a record of the mountains wearing down even as they grew.

olig-002.title: The Andes grow into a great mountain chain
olig-002.text: South America's western edge changed its geometry, and a mountain chain answered. Subduction, the sinking of an ocean plate beneath a continent, turned to run more directly into the coast, and the Andes first became a major mountain chain. About 30 million years ago the Andean orogeny, the long mountain-building episode along the margin, was rearranged on a continental scale. The changed subduction fed more volcanism, and the Western Cordillera of the Central Andes began to grow.

olig-004.title: Baikal's rift starts pulling apart again
olig-004.text: In the heart of Siberia, the crust began to stretch once more. Rifting in the Baikal Rift Zone resumed in the Oligocene. Over time the stretching formed graben basins, sunken troughs dropped between faults.

olig-005.title: Carnivorans seize the top predator roles
olig-005.text: In the Eocene, the top hunters had been oxyaenids and mesonychians. In the Oligocene, carnivorans took their place, led by the cat-like nimravids. Across the Old World, dogs, nimravids, bears, weasels and raccoons began to replace the older creodonts. The predator families that still rule land today were settling into their jobs.

olig-006.title: Desmostylians take to Oligocene seas
olig-006.text: Desmostylians were marine mammals with no living descendants, and they make their first appearance in the Oligocene. Early forms such as Behemotops are known from rocks of this epoch. The group did well. By the Late Oligocene it reached its highest diversity, with about nine species.

olig-010.title: Grasses leave the wetlands as forests shrink
olig-010.text: As the planet cooled, the forests lost ground. Tropical broadleaf forests shrank back to the equatorial belt, and grasslands expanded around the world. By the early Oligocene, tropical forests in North America and Eurasia had given way to dry woodland and wide grasslands. In South America the cooler climate spread savanna, open country with scattered trees. Grasses themselves changed address. They moved out of their old habitats at the edges of wetlands and into open land. Falling carbon dioxide favored C4 photosynthesis, a way of fixing carbon typical of grasses that works well when the gas is scarce. Even so, by the end of the epoch grass was still not common enough to make modern savannas. The open landscapes shaped the animals living in them. Cooling and spreading grassland favored the evolution of larger mammals, a trend that would run on through the Miocene.

olig-013.title: The Obik Sea drains and Europe meets Asia
olig-013.text: For a long time a shallow sea, the Obik Sea, kept Europe and Asia apart. Early in the Oligocene it retreated, and the two landmasses gained a lasting land connection. The cause was falling sea level, which closed the Turgai Strait that ran across it. With the water gone, Europe lay open to Asian mammals. The consequences arrived quickly, in the faunal upheaval described in {{ref:olig-020}}.

olig-014.title: Oi-2 glaciation drops the sea to a record low
olig-014.text: Growing Antarctic ice locked up so much water that the sea fell about 75 metres, the largest drop of the past 100 million years. Several pulses of glaciation struck in the middle Oligocene, around a shift in oxygen isotopes called Oi-2. Rivers cut into the exposed continental shelves, leaving gaps in marine rock records worldwide. Lesser turnovers of animal life came at the same time.

olig-015.title: Paratethys turns into a giant airless sea
olig-015.text: A northern arm of the Tethys, the Paratethys, covered much of central and eastern Europe in the Oligocene. Then a sea-level drop and the rise of Alpine mountain chains partly cut it off. Poorly connected to the world ocean, it became stratified, with layers of water that did not mix. Its depths turned anoxic, starved of oxygen. Sand from the rising mountains buried organic matter in the Maykop Suite, now a source of hydrocarbons around the Black Sea. The Menilite Formation still preserves its deep-sea fish and microbial mats.

olig-020.title: The Grande Coupure: Asia's mammals overrun Europe
olig-020.text: Around 33.5 million years ago, Europe's mammals turned over so sharply that the event got a French name meaning 'great break': the Grande Coupure. Before it, Europe had its own cast. Native artiodactyls, palaeothere perissodactyls, and adapid and omomyid primates dominated the landscape. Then falling sea level closed the Turgai Strait, the seaway described in {{ref:olig-013}}. Asian rhinos and ruminants walked in, and native species went extinct. Asian animals replaced most European mammals. Only some endemic rodent and marsupial families held on. The break brought widespread extinction, and the timing can be read in the rocks. The first Asian immigrants show up in northwest European records about 350,000 years after the break began. The sources differ slightly on placement: the Oligocene's own account puts it at the very start of the epoch.

olig-022.title: The Atacama begins its long drought
olig-022.text: The Atacama may be Earth's oldest desert. Its drying began with a proto-Humboldt Current, a cold coastal flow set up when the passage between Tasmania and Antarctica opened about 33 million years ago. After that, humid air was generally lacking there, apart from brief wetter spells.

olig-025.title: Greenland stops drifting and an Arctic orogeny ends
olig-025.text: Greenland once moved as a plate of its own, drifting north and rotating anticlockwise. About 33 million years ago that changed. Seafloor spreading in the Labrador Sea and Baffin Bay ceased and shifted to the northeast Atlantic. With the spreading stopped, the Eurekan orogeny, a mountain-building episode in the Arctic, came to a close. By the late Oligocene the boundary between North America and Eurasia ran along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, and Greenland had rejoined North America. One account dates the end of Labrador Sea spreading somewhat earlier.

olig-026.title: The Tasman Gateway opens a southern seaway
olig-026.text: Australia had been drifting slowly away from Antarctica since the Jurassic. About 33 million years ago, at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary, the Tasman Gateway between them opened, and abrupt cooling followed. The opening came in stages. Shallow channels south of Tasmania appeared in the Eocene, and deep-ocean routes followed from the mid Oligocene. One estimate puts a deep channel in place by the end of the early Oligocene. On land, southeastern Australia became a place of high rainfall and swamps.

olig-028.title: An asteroid strikes Arctic Devon Island
olig-028.text: An impactor about 2 km wide struck Devon Island in Arctic Canada, leaving the Haughton crater about 23 km across. The blast exposed rock from as deep as 1,700 m. Its age is unsettled. The crater's own record gives 31–32 million years, but other analyses place it in the Eocene, at 39 million years.

olig-030.title: Aegyptopithecus and the primates of the Fayum
olig-030.text: In Egypt's Fayum, about 30.2–29.5 million years ago, lived Aegyptopithecus, a catarrhine the size of a howler monkey. It predates the split between apes and Old World monkeys. Its home, the Jebel Qatrani Formation, records tropical forests, swamps and rivers draining north into the Tethys Sea. The formation holds over a dozen primate genera and early elephants such as Phiomia and Moeritherium.

olig-032.title: A current wraps Antarctica in cold water
olig-032.text: A ring of ocean now spins endlessly around Antarctica, and it may have started spinning about 30 million years ago. A steady circumpolar current probably did not form before then. A shallow flow at the Eocene–Oligocene boundary may have started a proto-current, but it was too shallow to circle the continent in earnest. Deep-sea cores south of New Zealand show cold deep currents by the early Oligocene. Once the gateways around Antarctica opened, the current kept cold water circling the continent. It also strengthened the formation of Antarctic Bottom Water, the cold, dense water that sinks to the ocean floor. Fossil evidence places its full establishment later, about 23 million years ago, after the Drake Passage opened fully and the Tasman Gateway deepened. The timing is disputed because it rests on the contested opening of the Drake Passage, described in {{ref:olig-048}}. Researchers also still debate how much the current drove Oligocene cooling.

olig-033.title: The brontotheres disappear
olig-033.text: The brontotheres were large hoofed mammals, and about 30 million years ago they went extinct. The Oligocene's own account places their end in the earliest part of the epoch. Either way, a familiar group of big plant-eaters left the stage as the world cooled.

olig-034.title: The Caspian Sea basin takes shape
olig-034.text: The Caspian Sea has deep roots. It is estimated to be about 30 million years old, which makes its basin a product of the Oligocene. Its later story, as it was cut off from the open sea, comes in {{ref:mioc-157}}.

olig-036.title: Ethiopian Traps flood the Horn of Africa with lava
olig-036.text: About 350,000 cubic kilometres of lava erupted around 30 million years ago across Ethiopia, northeast Sudan and southwest Yemen. The source was the Afar mantle plume, a rising column of hot rock, hitting the base of Africa's lithosphere. The lava came out of fissures, layer upon layer, and built the flood-basalt plateau of the Ethiopian Highlands. From 30 to 10 million years ago, shield volcanoes added another 1,000–2,000 m on top. The eruptions coincided with the start of rifting along the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden, told in {{ref:olig-041}}.

olig-041.title: Arabia begins to tear away from Africa
olig-041.text: For most of the Phanerozoic, Arabia was simply part of the African plate. In the Oligocene it began to split away. Rifting of the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden began around 30 million years ago, alongside the Ethiopian flood basalts. It started in the southern Red Sea in the mid Oligocene. By the late Oligocene it had spread along the whole Red Sea–Gulf of Suez system. The Gulf of Suez Rift stayed active from about 28 million years ago to the end of the Miocene. One account dates the final separation of Africa and Arabia to about 25 million years ago.

olig-042.title: The Rio Grande rift begins to stretch
olig-042.text: In what is now the American Southwest, the crust started pulling apart about 30 million years ago, opening the Rio Grande rift. An intense phase of rifting followed from 30 to 20 million years ago, with the crust sliding apart along low-angle faults.

olig-043.title: A spreading ridge meets California and the San Andreas is born
olig-043.text: About 30 million years ago, the spreading ridge between the Pacific and Farallon plates reached North America's subduction zone. The San Andreas Fault began to form. The first ridge segment entered the subduction zone near Baja California about 28 million years ago. As the Murray and Mendocino fracture zones arrived, strike-slip motion began, with plates grinding sideways past each other. Basin and Range extension started too. Volcanism ended south of the Cascades, and many western North American terranes, crustal blocks added to the continent, rotated clockwise.

olig-035.title: Dominican amber freezes a lost forest
olig-035.text: Dominican amber, 30–10 million years old, is nearly always clear and rich in inclusions, the remains of living things trapped in the resin. Those inclusions let scientists reconstruct a vanished tropical forest in detail.

olig-046.title: La Garita, one of Earth's greatest eruptions
olig-046.text: The eruption that formed La Garita Caldera in Colorado was among the largest and most powerful known in Earth's history. It blasted out the Fish Canyon Tuff, about 5,000 cubic kilometres of ash-flow deposit. The ground then collapsed into a caldera, a huge crater left by the emptied magma chamber. It was one of many calderas in a huge ignimbrite flare-up across Colorado, Utah and Nevada from 40 to 18 million years ago. Its crystals have a second life. Sanidine from the tuff, astronomically dated to 28.175 million years, is a reference standard for argon–argon dating.

olig-048.title: The Drake Passage parts South America from Antarctica
olig-048.text: South America and Antarctica were once joined at their tips. Seafloor spreading along the Scotia Ridge finally parted them by 28 million years ago, forming the Drake Passage. South America became an island continent and began drifting north toward North America. Together with the Tasmanian Gateway in {{ref:olig-026}}, the new opening reshaped Oligocene ocean currents. It may have helped trigger Antarctic glaciation, though models suggest falling carbon dioxide mattered more. The date is one of the most disputed in this chapter. Published estimates for the opening range from 49 to 17 million years ago. One study finds deep-water flow possible by about 31 million years ago. Sources still disagree whether the passage opened near the start or near the end of the Oligocene.

olig-049.title: The first pelicans
olig-049.text: Pelicans have an old pedigree. The first members of the group appear in the fossil record about 28 million years ago. That puts the big-billed fishers in the middle of the Oligocene.

olig-050.title: Paraceratherium, the largest land mammal ever
olig-050.text: Paraceratherium was the largest land mammal that ever lived, and it appears in the fossil record about 28 million years ago. This hornless rhino relative weighed up to 15–20 tonnes. Giant indricotheres like it stood up to 6 metres at the shoulder in Eurasia. They were exceptions. Most Oligocene mammals ran much smaller than their Eocene predecessors, and these giants bucked the trend.

olig-052.title: Caviomorph rodents spread through South America
olig-052.text: Caviomorph rodents, the group of South American rodents, had reached Patagonia by the early Oligocene. By the Late Oligocene they had split into all four main lineages. Some grew large and competed with native hoofed mammals, perhaps helping those animals' slow decline after the early Oligocene.

olig-053.title: Embrithopods leave the record
olig-053.text: Embrithopods were an order of mammals that lived only in Afro-Arabia, a branch of the continent's homegrown fauna. Their last record comes from the latest Oligocene, and after that the order is gone. One timeline sets their extinction earlier, at about 30 million years ago.

olig-054.title: Proailurus, the first cat
olig-054.text: The cat family starts with Proailurus. This first felid arose in Asia in the late Oligocene and spread to Europe, and the earliest felid fossils come from Oligocene Europe. Timelines date the first cats to about 30 or 25 million years ago. The saber-toothed look came later: the first cat with saber-tooth features is Pseudaelurus, from the Miocene.

olig-056.title: The first elephantimorphs
olig-056.text: The lineage that would give rise to mastodons and modern elephants made its first appearance in the Late Oligocene. These were the elephantimorphs, the branch of proboscideans that includes both. One timeline dates the first true elephants to about 26 million years ago, though the elephant family proper is traced in {{ref:mioc-116}}.

olig-058.title: Notoungulates grow teeth that never stop
olig-058.text: Several South American notoungulate families separately evolved high-crowned cheek teeth that kept growing throughout life. They arrived at the same solution independently. From the Late Oligocene on, such species made up most notoungulates.

olig-060.title: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first forms
olig-060.text: The West Antarctic Ice Sheet first formed about 27 million years ago, probably fed partly by glaciers from the older East Antarctic Ice Sheet. It is a marine ice sheet. Most of its ice rests on rock and sediment well below sea level, ground that would be ocean floor without the ice.

olig-061.title: A late Oligocene warm spell
olig-061.text: Between 26.5 and 24 million years ago, the late Oligocene probably warmed, despite low carbon dioxide. Temperatures rose slightly but stayed well below earlier Paleogene levels, and Antarctica stayed heavily glaciated. Pollen from the Tibetan Plateau records the warming. Lanternfish, once confined to shelf seas, spread into the open ocean.

olig-062.title: The Farallon Plate breaks up
olig-062.text: About 26 million years ago, the Farallon Plate broke up into the Cocos and Nazca plates. Subduction sped up. Volcanism revived in the Central Andes, and the volcanic arc broadened to about 250 km. Activity rose sharply along the Andes, and the modern volcanic arc and tectonic regime took shape. At the Paleogene–Neogene boundary, Pacific–Farallon spreading stopped and the plate split again into today's Nazca and Cocos plates.

olig-063.title: Tibet rises and the South Asian monsoon strengthens
olig-063.text: The South Asian monsoon intensified sharply around 25.8 million years ago. The trigger was the rising Tibetan Plateau. The monsoon itself was not new. Tibetan pollen shows it had already developed by the late Oligocene, and the plateau's growth turned it up. A higher plateau meant a stronger seasonal swing in the winds, and the same link between Tibet and the monsoons returns throughout the Miocene.

olig-064.title: Rukwapithecus and the earliest apes and monkeys
olig-064.text: In the Rukwa Rift of Tanzania, the Nsungwe Formation is about 25.2 million years old. It yields Rukwapithecus, interpreted as the earliest known ape, or hominoid. The same beds hold Nsungwepithecus, an early Old World monkey. So by then the two groups had already split. That fits molecular estimates placing the split at about 25–30 million years ago, though early catarrhine relationships remain uncertain. The finds reach into a poorly sampled stretch of time, and tectonic changes in East Africa may have shaped how both groups diversified.

olig-065.title: Central America begins to close its seaway
olig-065.text: A long chain of volcanoes started the job of joining two continents. By the Oligocene, the Central American volcanic arc began colliding with northwestern South America. That collision, which would eventually close the Central American Seaway, started about 25 million years ago. The process ran for millions of years, through the closure of the deep seaway in {{ref:mioc-094}} to the final link in {{ref:plio-056}}.

olig-068.title: Riversleigh starts recording a lost rainforest
olig-068.text: Riversleigh in Queensland is Australia's most famous fossil site, and its story begins in the late Oligocene. Some of its fossils are 25 million years old. Its limestones formed in what was once a very wet rainforest, a far cry from the dry country there now. The site keeps recording life for millions of years, as {{ref:mioc-019}} shows.

olig-069.title: The Sea of Japan begins to open
olig-069.text: Around 25 million years ago the Sea of Japan began to open. As it widened, Japan pulled away from the Asian mainland and took the form of today's island arc. The opening continued into the Miocene, as {{ref:mioc-079}} describes.

olig-066.title: East Africa starts to split open
olig-066.text: Mount Elgon, at least 24 million years old, is East Africa's oldest known extinct volcano, and it stands at the start of a great tearing. The East African Rift began to develop around the start of the Miocene, 25–22 million years ago. Its fires began earlier. Volcanism started on the central Ethiopian plateau around 30 million years ago, long before any rifting there. In northern Kenya, rifting and volcanism began around the same time. Then the crack worked its way south. It reached southern Kenya by 12 million years ago and northern Tanzania by 8 million years ago. The rift would go on to reshape the landscape of eastern Africa, the setting for much of the human story later in this course.

olig-074.title: Seals arrive and nautiloids vanish
olig-074.text: The earliest pinnipeds, the group that includes seals, appeared about 24 million years ago, near the end of the Oligocene. Their spread left a curious pattern in the fossil record. From the Oligocene on, nautiloids vanished from each region as pinnipeds appeared there. Wherever the new marine mammals arrived, the ancient shelled hunters of the sea disappeared.

olig-076.title: Creodonts retreat to Africa
olig-076.text: At the end of the Oligocene, creodonts died out everywhere except Africa and the Middle East. The old predator order, long pushed aside by carnivorans, hung on only in that corner of the world. Its final end is told in {{ref:mioc-063}}.

olig-077.title: A deep freeze closes the Oligocene
olig-077.text: A deep glaciation lasting 400,000 years marks the Oligocene–Miocene boundary at McMurdo Sound and King George Island in Antarctica. The boundary rests on regional shifts from the warmer late Oligocene to the cooler Miocene. The Miocene opened with the Mi-1 cool event around 23 million years ago, as Antarctica's ice sheets expanded.

olig-078.title: The pyrotheres die out
olig-078.text: The pyrotheres were a South American mammal order known since the Early Eocene. They were among the continent's distinctive native mammals, alongside astrapotheres, litopterns and notoungulates. Their last record comes at the end of the Oligocene.

openers.oligocene-epoch: About 33.9 million years ago, ice began to build up on Antarctica, and Earth entered the ice age it is still in. The Oligocene is the story of that cooling and everything it touched. Tropical forests shrank toward the equator and grasslands spread around the world. The sea drained from the Obik Sea, joining Europe to Asia, and Asian mammals poured west in a turnover called the 'great break'. Meanwhile Africa pushed into Eurasia, the Alps rose, and the Andes became a major mountain chain.
openers.neogene-period: The Neogene opens in a world that was getting cooler, drier and more seasonal. Africa's plant diversity fell sharply at the start, and grasses kept spreading until they dominated much of the world while forests dwindled. Mountains rose on two continents: the Andes lifted fastest in this time, and sediment from the rising Himalaya built the vast Bengal Fan. In the sea, whales and dolphins reached their greatest diversity and kelp forests first appeared. On land, apes evolved and spread across the Old World.
openers.miocene-epoch: Apes first evolved in the early Miocene, then diversified and spread across the Old World. Around them the world was turning seasonal. Global cooling gave the East Asian Summer Monsoon its modern form, and grasses came to dominate much of the land. The crust was busy too: the Andes rose fastest in this epoch, and the Tian Shan and Altai mountains formed. The oceans gained new life, from kelp forests to the greatest variety of whales and dolphins Earth has known.

reviews.oligocene-epoch: Ice on Antarctica set the tone for the whole Oligocene. Falling carbon dioxide froze the poles, and the growing ice dropped sea level about 75 metres, which closed the Turgai Strait and let Asian mammals overrun Europe in the Grande Coupure. Opening gateways south of Australia and South America let a current circle Antarctica, while grasses spread and favored larger mammals such as Paraceratherium. Meanwhile the crust broke and buckled: Arabia began to pull away from Africa, the East African Rift began to form, and the San Andreas Fault began to grow.
